title: Labour markets & wages
examples: How does the supply of labour affect wages?
What is the role of a trade union in wage negotiation?
If the minimum wage increases, what happens to employment?

explain.say: Today we will explore how wages are determined in a market.
The interaction between labour supply and demand sets the equilibrium wage.
A minimum wage is a legal floor set by the government for pay.
Trade unions organize workers to negotiate better pay and conditions.
In a real-life scenario, imagine a local bakery needing more staff.
A common mistake is assuming that a minimum wage always increases employment.

items: Minimum wage can affect hiring decisions.
Businesses might reduce hours instead of staff.
The effect depends on market elasticity.

faq.q: If the minimum wage is set too high, what happens to businesses?
faq.a: Businesses might find it unprofitable to hire as many workers. They may reduce their overall operations or cut staff hours.
asks: What is the impact on employment levels?

faq.q: How do unions actually negotiate wages with employers?
faq.a: Unions negotiate on behalf of a group of workers through collective bargaining. They aim for an agreement that benefits the majority of their members.
asks: Do unions just ask for more money?
What is the process of collective bargaining?

faq.q: Is the wage determined only by the supply and demand of labour?
faq.a: While supply and demand are key, other factors like government regulation and union power also play a role. These factors shift the equilibrium.
asks: Are wages set by the government or the market?
What are the limiting factors for wages?

faq.q: What is the difference between a minimum wage and a negotiated wage?
faq.a: The minimum wage is a legal baseline set by law. A negotiated wage is an agreement reached between workers and employers through bargaining.
asks: Can employers pay less than the minimum wage?
Is negotiation always better than a law?

faq.q: Does the labour supply curve slope upwards or downwards?
faq.a: The labour supply curve slopes upwards because, generally, as wages increase, more people are willing to work or work more hours.
asks: Why does supply increase with wage?
What is the relationship between wage and willingness to work?

facts: The equilibrium wage is where the quantity of labour supplied equals the quantity demanded.
A minimum wage acts as a price floor, setting the lowest legal rate of pay.
Trade unions use collective bargaining to improve wages and working conditions.
If the minimum wage is set above equilibrium, a surplus of labour can occur.

quiz.say: If the demand for labour increases significantly, what is the most likely immediate effect on the equilibrium wage?

options.show: Increase only if unions are involved
options.say: Increase only if unions are involved

quiz.why: Higher demand for labour at any given wage means employers must compete more, pushing wages up.

wrong.1: This is wrong because increased demand signals that labour is more valuable to firms.
wrong.2: This is wrong because the market is not in equilibrium if demand changes without a wage adjustment.
wrong.3: This is wrong because the fundamental law of supply and demand dictates a wage rise regardless of unions.

quiz.say: If the government imposes a minimum wage significantly above the market equilibrium wage, what economic outcome is expected?
quiz.why: A price floor above equilibrium causes the quantity supplied of labour to exceed the quantity demanded, creating a surplus.

wrong.0: This is wrong because the immediate effect is on the labour market balance, not necessarily capital investment.
wrong.2: This is wrong because the excess supply of labour means not all workers can be employed at that rate.
wrong.3: This is wrong because the law dictates the wage, preventing compression, though other effects may occur.

quiz.say: Which factor is primarily responsible for giving workers the power to negotiate wages collectively?

options.show: The government setting the minimum wage
options.say: The government setting the minimum wage

quiz.why: Unions organize workers, giving them a collective voice and bargaining power that individuals lack.

wrong.1: This is wrong because the government sets a floor, but unions negotiate above that floor.
wrong.2: This is wrong because high supply generally puts downward pressure on wages, not empowering negotiation.
wrong.3: This is wrong because while high demand helps, it is the organized group that formalizes the bargaining power.
